Measured on one RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell · Fast mode · 11 November 2026

Do batching or extra transformers help
when every chunk is 10 seconds?

Exactly five independent 10-second chunks per video. Same portrait, audio slices, seeds, two denoising steps and output settings in every configuration.

Results · Watch videos · SM activity and overlap · How we measured · Evidence

One transformer + two VAEs remains fastest.

Batch-two on 1T/2V took 212.68 seconds, versus 208.93 seconds for sequential denoising: 1.8% more time. The fastest measured layout was 1 transformer + 2 VAEs · sequential denoising at 208.93 seconds. These are three-run means for the complete 50-second video: original generation plus a separately timed, lossless timestamp correction of about 0.06 seconds.

The original assembly started video 20.996 ms after audio. A lossless remux now puts both streams at zero and adds about 0.06 seconds per video. Compressed video and audio payloads are unchanged. Original files and generation timings are preserved; each row shows generation and the separately measured correction. Repair evidence and commands.

Batch size two does not mean two chunks per video. It uses the five fixed chunks as [0,1] → [2,3] → [4]. VAE workers decode completed chunks while the transformer continues. Two transformer copies take independent chunks from the same five-chunk queue.

Batching was genuine: the five chunks used three sampler calls and six main transformer forwards, versus five calls and ten forwards without batching. The paired calls processed both chunks together; all fast-attention counters passed with zero fallbacks. Fewer calls did not translate into a shorter complete-video time.

Batch handoff refinement

The initial batch implementation took 212.59 seconds on average. Its four paired chunk handoffs each stored both batch items in their backing storage (51.1 MB per file). We compacted each saved item to 25.5 MB, verified bit-identical tensor values on CPU, and repeated the full warmup plus three videos. The primary batch row above uses the corrected compact handoff. Initial runs remain in the downloads and raw evidence.

What consumed the time?

With two transformers and two VAEs, denoising finished 4.42 seconds earlier. The remaining decode/assembly tail took 7.42 seconds longer, leaving the complete video 3.00 seconds slower. Batching changed denoising completion by only 0.36 seconds and also lengthened the tail.

Output validation

All 90 measured MP4s passed integrity and frame/timestamp checks (6 distinct byte sequences fully decoded; identical copies verified by SHA-256): 15 complete videos and 75 component chunks, including the initial batch handoff. All 75 measured latent pairs are finite and their video latents are bit-identical to baseline. All delivered full videos are byte-identical across the tested configurations and repeats.

Complete videos: 1,200 frames, 24 fps, 1080 × 1920, 50 seconds. Audio alignment checks found zero lag at 8 kHz, with minimum waveform correlation 0.999723. Export uses the supplied source audio; generated audio latents are not used.

3. What the GPU was doing

One 10-second chunk already reached 96.2% SMs Active before any VAE started. Two transformers raised this to about 99.7%, while Tensor Active rose only from 60.7% to 62.5%. The copies did overlap, but useful end-to-end speed did not improve.

Nsight captures are separate diagnostic reruns of the same five-by-10-second workload. Their runtimes are excluded from the timing table above. Instrumentation can change scheduling; overlap figures describe the profiled replays.

The table’s SM averages cover the initial denoising period before the first transformer call finishes, while VAE workers are idle. Kernel-overlap durations cover the complete measured denoising phase.

Profiled configurationSMs Active before VAESM Issue before VAETensor Active before VAETwo T calls in flightTwo T kernels simultaneouslyTransformer + VAE kernel overlap
sequential 1t2v96.20%28.46%60.74%0.00 s0.00 s38.73 s
concurrent 2t1v99.72%29.99%62.49%133.65 s39.91 s10.36 s
concurrent 2t2v99.76%30.00%62.53%133.76 s39.50 s11.08 s

In the two-transformer/two-VAE replay, transformer kernels overlapped for 39.50 seconds, despite both transformer calls being in flight for 133.76 seconds. Transformer–VAE kernel overlap fell from 38.73 seconds in the baseline to 11.08 seconds. This is consistent with the unprofiled result: a small denoising gain is outweighed by a longer decode tail.

Trace integrity and profiler warnings

Each capture includes all ten expected measured stage ranges, 250 SA2 and 250 SA3 attention launches, and approximately 1,000 SM samples per second throughout the stage window. Each profiled output is byte-identical to its matching original unprofiled assembly, before the lossless delivery timestamp correction. Nsight warns that not all NVTX events might have been collected; the ten required benchmark ranges are present. Non-GPU child processes also produce no-CUDA/no-NVTX warnings. CPU scheduling capture was disabled, so the report uses CUDA kernel intervals and explicit synchronized stage ranges, rather than inferred CPU scheduling activity.

Chart time is elapsed generation time. Each output video itself lasts 50 seconds.

Wide overlapping bars show calls in flight, including time they wait. They do not establish simultaneous kernel execution.

These are selected isolated kernel instances, not an average across the video. The accompanying Nsight Systems launch evidence records maximum shared memory and registers for the dominant kernels in the actual pipeline.

Selected INT8 matrix kernels reached up to 94.9% SM throughput; another reached 90.3% DRAM throughput. Their roughly 16.7% warp occupancy does not imply that the remaining GPU capacity can run several additional copies efficiently. Register and shared-memory limits allow only one of these GEMM blocks per SM.

A specific fast-kernel tuning opportunity

The captured SageAttention3 launch uses 170 blocks on this 188-SM GPU. The installed fast-kernel source hard-codes 170. Each block requests 100,352 bytes (98 KiB) of shared memory, against 100 KiB per SM, leaving insufficient shared memory for a second copy of that block on the same SM. This limits how much two such kernels can overlap productively.

Changing the launch to account for the actual SM count is an untested tuning candidate, not a measured speedup. It could also reduce room for concurrent VAE work. The benchmark kept the existing fast kernel unchanged. Source and launch evidence.

Definitions and profiling limitations: NVIDIA Nsight Systems guide; NVIDIA Nsight Compute profiling guide. The initial thread-scoped NCU filter captured no kernels because inference runs in another thread; the successful capture uses process-scoped NVTX filtering. NCU replays selected isolated kernels and can serialize work; its times are not concurrent pipeline timings.

4. Fixed workload and fair comparison

GPUOne RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Workstation Edition, 97,887 MiB reported memory / 95.59 GiB, 638 MiB driver reservation, 188 SMs, 600 W
Video contractExactly five 10-second chunks; 240 delivered frames each; 1,200 frames / 50 seconds
Native model frames243 frames per chunk, trimmed by the existing export path to 240
Model and optimizationH3 Pika Flex; two steps; SA2 first step, SA3 FP4 second step; NVFP4 VAE projections
Anchors and seedsOriginal portrait at both native endpoints for each independent chunk; seeds 9901 through 9905
DimensionsNative 736×1280, cropped to 720×1280, exported at 1080×1920
AudioSame 49.408-second reference recording, padded with 0.592 seconds of trailing silence to 50 seconds; five identical 10-second slices across configurations
PreparationGPU text/image/audio conditioning prepared once and reused byte-for-byte; text encoder process exits before resident generation workers start
Timing boundaryFive prepared chunks dispatched through final assembled MP4; includes latent serialization, IPC, decode, encode and mux. Excludes initial preparation, warmup and post-run validation.
RepetitionsOne complete warmup and three measured full videos; no best-run selection
OrderSequential 1T/2V → initial batch 1T/2V → concurrent 2T/1V → concurrent 2T/2V → compact batch 1T/2V; no randomized blocks
GPU checksThree consecutive idle host samples before each fresh workload; continuous process-ownership checks throughout
ProfilingSeparate full-workload Nsight Systems replays; 1 kHz GPU metrics; NCU isolated kernels; never included in performance means

What is held constant

All layouts reuse byte-identical GPU-prepared conditioning, then release the text encoder. The transformer and VAE workers remain alive through the full warmup and three measured videos. Each worker owns its model copy. The existing fast VAE path retains its quantized projection cache on CPU and copies those projections to a request-local GPU cache for each decode; this is held constant across layouts. The memory table separately reports transformer and VAE residency accounting. MPS is enabled with the same 100% active-thread allowance. Dispatch queues permit stage overlap; each VAE decodes one chunk at a time.

Warmup and repetitions use the same fixed inputs. This is a resident replay benchmark, not a production service or a randomized cross-day experiment. Small differences should not be treated as a precise long-term gain.

Quality limitations

Frame/audio integrity, waveform timing, reproducibility and visual differences are checked. Those checks do not rate semantic quality, natural motion, lip synchronization or seam acceptability. Native first/last-image conditioning does not force exact endpoint pixels; export trims the native 243 frames to 240.
